The TypeScript decoders take a string, so bytes that aren't UTF-8 never reach them: the caller's UTF-8 decoding rejects them first. TypeScript is held to invalid_json at the root; Rust and Go are compared on every field.
Every language rejects 2^63 with out_of_range_integer at the same path, but the error names the range the language holds: 64 bits in Rust and Go, 2^53 - 1 in TypeScript.
Every language rejects -2^63 - 1 with out_of_range_integer at the same path, but the error names the range the language holds: 64 bits in Rust and Go, 2^53 - 1 in TypeScript.
A TypeScript number holds integers exactly only up to 2^53 - 1, where Rust and Go hold 64 bits. TypeScript rejects 2^63 - 1 with out_of_range_integer rather than round it.

The TypeScript decoders take a string, so bytes that aren't UTF-8 never reach them: the caller's UTF-8 decoding rejects them first. TypeScript is held to invalid_json at the root; Rust and Go are compared on every field.
Go decodes a number field to a json.Number and writes it back as it was read, 1e-07, where Rust and TypeScript write the double as 1e-7. Same value, so the canonical bytes are equal.

Each language spells a decoded number its own way when it encodes it again: Rust writes 150.0, Go keeps 1.50E+2 as it was read, TypeScript writes 150. The value is the same, so the canonical bytes are.

extra holds any JSON value. Go keeps such a value as the bytes it read, TypeScript writes its keys in input order and Rust in code point order. Same members, so the canonical bytes, sorted by UTF-16 code units, are equal.
